title: Vatican I, 1870
hookLine: the pope is protected from error only when solemnly defining faith or morals for the whole Church, rarely used

cards: A pope says he likes a film. A pope gives an interview on a plane. A pope picks a soccer team.

Somewhere, within the hour, a headline asks whether Catholics now have to agree with him. The question comes from a word the First Vatican Council defined, and it's often misheard. It doesn't mean the pope is never wrong.
It means something much smaller and much stranger. Today's word: infallibility.

teach.b: Start with what it isn't. Infallibility is not sinlessness; popes go to confession too. It isn't about a pope's opinions, his homilies, his interviews or his politics either.
Now, what the council actually said.

teach.h: EX CATHEDRA: FAITH OR MORALS, FOR ALL.
teach.b: Its constitution on the papacy, called Pastor Aeternus, teaches that when the Roman Pontiff speaks ex cathedra, from the chair, meaning when, as shepherd and teacher of all Christians, he defines a teaching on faith or morals to be held by the whole Church, he is kept from error by the help God promised to Peter.
Every one of those conditions has to be there. Next, the reason given.
The council pointed to Jesus's words at the Last Supper, in the Douay-Rheims: "But I have prayed for thee, that thy faith fail not: and thou, being once converted, confirm thy brethren."
And the same document says the Holy Spirit was not promised so the popes could make known new teaching, but so they could guard and faithfully explain what was handed down.
A guardrail, not an engine. Finally, how often.
Catholic teachers point out that solemn definitions like this are rare; the example people usually give is Pope Pius the Twelfth defining Mary's Assumption.
Other Christians, Orthodox and Protestant, do not accept this teaching, and some Catholics at the council itself argued that defining it was unwise.

how: Catholics distinguish a pope's solemn definitions, which the Church holds as infallible, from his ordinary teaching, homilies and personal opinions, and Catholic catechisms explain the narrow conditions set by the First Vatican Council.

o: the belief that a pope can never sin at all
kept from error when solemnly defining for all
the duty to agree with every word a pope says

p: from the chair: a solemn definition

games.q: a pope shares his view on a film in an interview. a friend asks if Catholics must now agree. what's the answer by Vatican I's terms?
o: yes, a pope can't be wrong.
no, it's not a solemn definition of faith or morals.
only if he says it twice.
games.why: Vatican I limits infallibility to solemn definitions on faith or morals for the whole Church, so an opinion on a film falls outside it.

practice: Walk slowly through the conditions, one per breath: the pope, speaking as teacher of all Christians, defining, faith or morals, for the whole Church.
Then let go of everything that falls outside them: the interviews, the opinions, the plane rides. If you pray, pray for the pope in Jesus's words, that his faith fail not.

wordCard.voice: Infallibility. Protection from error when the pope solemnly defines faith or morals for the whole Church; not sinlessness, and not his every word. Today's word.

orig.note: the Latin noun behind the English word; Vatican I wrote in Latin.

carryVoice: Your line: rarer than people think. All five conditions at once, or it isn't this. See you tomorrow.
